chunks: " volatile is a qualifier that tells the compiler: this variable can change in ways you can't see from the code, so don't optimize away or cache its accesses.
Every read in the source must be an actual read from memory, and every write an actual write, in the order I wrote them.
The reason it matters is that optimizing compilers assume that, unless my code writes to a variable, its value doesn't change. So if I write while (!
flag) {} and flag is set by an interrupt, the compiler can read flag once into a register and loop forever on the stale copy.
That's the classic 'works in debug, hangs in release' bug. Marking flag volatile forces a fresh read every iteration. I use it in three places.
First, memory-mapped hardware registers, where reading a status register or writing a control register must really happen, every time, because it has side effects.
Second, variables shared between an ISR and main code. And third, busy-wait loops polling something the hardware updates. What I'd stress is what volatile doesn't do.
It doesn't make an operation atomic: counter++ on a volatile is still a read, an increment and a write, and an interrupt can land in the middle, so I'd disable interrupts around it or use atomics.
It doesn't synchronize threads on a multi-core system, and it doesn't act as a memory barrier.
So it's the right tool for hardware registers and ISR flags, and the wrong tool for general thread safety."
